tagline: A prairie drive linking two wetlands on the Central Flyway
intro: The Wetlands and Wildlife National Scenic Byway curves past Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira National Wildlife Refuge, crossing the Central Flyway in central Kansas. Kansas Tourism lays out a 77-mile drive from Hoisington to St. John, using K-4, K-156 and local roads. The byway organization identifies the wetlands as stopovers for millions of migrating birds each year, including waterfowl, shorebirds and whooping cranes.

At Cheyenne Bottoms, the struggle to direct water preceded the scenic route. The Koen Ditch project attempted to bring Arkansas River water to the basin for irrigation in 1900, but a flood washed the ditch out. Plans in the 1920s reversed the idea: drain the Bottoms for farmland. Downstream residents in Hutchinson protested that this would create flooding problems. Kansas created its Forestry, Fish and Game Commission in 1925 to develop and care for the Bottoms. Federal wildlife-restoration legislation in 1937 then made development funds available through taxes on sporting arms and ammunition.

Begin in Hoisington and head east on K-4 toward Cheyenne Bottoms. The route then turns south on NE 100 Avenue to K-156 before continuing along local roads toward Quivira. Beyond the refuge, it follows Raymond Road south and NE 70th Street west, finishing at US-281 just north of St. John.

moments.title: Cheyenne Bottoms
moments.text: The basin is natural; the divisions across it are engineered. Cheyenne Bottoms occupies a land sink, with its wetland pools separated by dikes. Historically, it has alternated between lake, mudflat and dry ground. A new canal from the Arkansas River arrived in 1957, but drought and competing water claims limited how much reached the wetland. Renovations in the 1990s subdivided the marshes to make them more self-sustaining, though water supply and water-level management remain critical problems. Migrating shorebirds feed on the mudflats. Blood Creek and Deception Creek feed the basin from the northwest; a canal brings another inflow from Walnut Creek.
moments.notice: Dikes divide the wetland into pools, with mudflats, ponds and islands beside them.

moments.title: Quivira National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Salt marshes distinguish Quivira, where Rattlesnake Creek supplies the main flow of water. Big Salt Marsh and Little Salt Marsh are shallow lakes, and 21 miles of constructed canals create additional marshland. The refuge was created in 1955. Its name comes from a fabled city of gold sought by Francisco Vásquez de Coronado in 1541. He spent a month with the Quivirans, ancestors of the Wichita tribe, before returning to New Mexico without gold. The refuge’s sand prairie combines plants from eastern tallgrass and western shortgrass prairie. Winter wheat and milo are also grown on refuge land, with part of the crop left for wildlife.

moments.title: St. John
moments.text: St. John began with a different name and a religious purpose. In 1875, William Bickerton of the Church of Jesus Christ founded a colony here called Zion Valley. By 1879 it had grown into a small town, and residents renamed it for Governor John P. St. John to gain favor in the contest for Stafford County’s seat. St. John remains the seat of Stafford County. The spelling became another civic project: residents secured a correction in 2015 after the Postal Service had changed the official listing to “Saint John” in the 1970s.
